evidence.claim: Walmart's 2025 annual report describes EDLP/EDLC as core to its strategy, reports approximately 270 million weekly customers globally, and generated total revenues of $681.0 billion in fiscal 2025.

Seneca's 2025 annual report states that products are sold under private label and brands through supermarkets, mass merchandisers, limited-assortment stores, club stores and dollar stores, and that it also packs canned and frozen vegetables under contract-packing agreements.

Seneca's 2025 annual report says the top ten customers represented approximately 53% of fiscal 2025 net sales and that its performance obligations include production of food products plus case, labeling, and storage services for some bill-and-hold sales.

Cal-Maine's fiscal 2025 Form 10-K states that Walmart Inc., including Sam's Club, accounted for 33.6%, 34.0%, and 34.2% of net sales across the disclosed fiscal years, and its sales include private-label specialty eggs.

Reynolds Consumer Products' 2025 annual report says it sells both branded and store-brand products and that three customers accounted for more than 10% of fiscal 2025 net revenue, with two affiliated customers representing 31% and 17%.
evidence.source_title: Reynolds Consumer Products Inc. 2025 Annual Report

memory_update.text: SENEA should be tracked as an underfollowed direct private-label/co-pack candidate for canned and frozen vegetables, with verification focused on customer concentration, co-pack revenue/deferred revenue, retailer channels, and seasonal working-capital risk.

CALM should be tracked as an underfollowed category-specific value-staples supplier where Walmart/Sam's Club concentration, private-label specialty eggs, food safety, flock health, and commodity pricing determine whether exposure is bottleneck-like or merely cyclical.

REYN should be tracked as a second-order specialty packaging/store-brand household consumables candidate; the key evidence gap is identifying top customers and separating branded from store-brand growth and margin contribution.

TreeHouse Foods was formerly the cleanest public private-label food manufacturing reference, but it was taken private in February 2026; future Layer 1 passes should search for remaining public peers and suppliers left behind after THS delisting.

For this node, retailer qualification, private-label contract duration, food-safety compliance, packaging/labeling services, and ability to meet Walmart/club/dollar-store service levels are more important screening variables than generic packaged-food revenue growth.

node: Private-label co-manufacturing, specialty packaging, and value-tier consumer staples inputs
summary: Layer 1B expands the node around retailer-qualified, food-safety-compliant, private-label and value-tier staples capacity. The best underfollowed mappings are not broad consumer-brand owners, but suppliers whose filings reveal direct exposure to mass merchants, club stores, dollar stores, store-brand programs, co-pack arrangements, or retailer-specific packaging formats. Walmart is included only as the reference demand anchor; the discovery lane prioritizes Seneca Foods, Cal-Maine Foods, and Reynolds Consumer Products as public suppliers where retailer qualification, volume service levels, packaging/labeling, commodity pass-through, and customer concentration may be the true bottleneck variables.
